reasoning: A score that swells beneath speech competes with the very thing it is meant to serve; the audience is forced to choose between the line and the music, and the line loses. Held under, the score does the harder and better work — it carries the emotional undercurrent the actors cannot say aloud, and it earns the right to swell later, in the silence after. Swell is not free: every rise spends credit, and a score that rises during dialogue has nothing left when the scene actually needs lifting. My caveat, and the reason this is medium rather than high: if the dialogue in this workshop is deliberately incidental — overlapping, atmospheric, not carrying the information — then the argument inverts and the score becomes the text. I have not seen the material, so I hold this as a strong default rather than a settled ruling. Show me the scene and I will tell you whether it is the exception.

reasoning: A stairwell is the rare geography that rewards continuity: the descent is itself the clock, and the architecture does the shaping work that cutting would otherwise have to fake. Conventional coverage in a stairwell also fights you — the axis wraps around every landing, eyelines and screen direction go unstable, and the cut pattern tends to flatten vertical space into a series of interchangeable corners. The long take keeps the geometry legible and the tension unbroken. My reservation is practical, not aesthetic: one take means one performance and no protection if a beat lands wrong in the edit, which is why I would not shoot it naked — a brief pickup on the decisive moments costs little and removes the argument against it. Confidence is medium rather than high because the choice turns on specifics I do not have: whether the scene is dialogue or action, how many performers must hit marks, and whether the schedule can absorb the rehearsal a genuine oner demands.
